fields.name: Frontend
fields.definition: The code that runs on the user's device and turns data into an interface they can see and use.
showsUp: Browsers, mobile web views and desktop shells.
Anywhere latency is felt directly by a person.
tradeoffs: You do not control the device, the network or the browser version.
Every byte you ship is paid for by the user.

areas.name: Rendering
areas.definition: How markup, styles and data become pixels, and where that work happens: server, build step or browser.
showsUp: Choosing between server-rendered, static and client-rendered pages.
Debugging a page that flashes or shifts as it loads.
tradeoffs: Rendering earlier improves first paint but can delay interactivity.
Mixing strategies per route adds mental overhead.

terms.name: Hydration
terms.definition: Attaching event handlers and state to server-rendered HTML so a static page becomes interactive.
showsUp: Server-rendered React, Vue and Svelte apps.
The gap where a button is visible but does nothing yet.
tradeoffs: The browser re-runs component code it already received as HTML.
Server and client output must match, or you get mismatch errors.

terms.name: Virtual DOM
terms.definition: An in-memory tree describing the UI, diffed against the previous one to work out the smallest real DOM update.
showsUp: React and similar libraries on every state change.
List rendering, where keys tell the diff which items moved.
tradeoffs: Diffing is work in itself; it is convenient, not free.
Unstable keys cause lost input state and needless re-renders.

areas.name: State
areas.definition: The data an interface remembers between renders, and the rules for who may read and change it.
showsUp: Form inputs, open menus, fetched data and the current URL.
Bugs where two parts of the screen disagree.
tradeoffs: Global state is easy to reach and hard to reason about.
Copying server data into client state creates a second source of truth.

terms.name: Reactivity
terms.definition: A system that tracks which code depends on which data and re-runs only that code when the data changes.
showsUp: Signals in Solid, Vue refs and Svelte runes.
Spreadsheet-style derived values that stay in sync.
tradeoffs: Dependencies are tracked implicitly, so a missed read means a stale UI.
Chains of derived values can be hard to trace when something updates unexpectedly.

terms.name: Stores
terms.definition: A shared container for state that lives outside any one component and notifies subscribers when it changes.
showsUp: Redux, Zustand and Pinia.
Auth status, carts and other data many screens need.
tradeoffs: Everything subscribed re-renders unless you select narrowly.
It is tempting to put local state there, which couples unrelated screens.

areas.name: Styling
areas.definition: How visual rules are written, scoped and kept consistent across an interface.
showsUp: CSS files, utility classes and component-scoped styles.
Theming, dark mode and responsive layout.
tradeoffs: Unscoped styles leak; fully scoped styles are harder to theme.
Runtime styling libraries cost render time.

terms.name: Cascade
terms.definition: The algorithm CSS uses to decide which declaration wins when several target the same element.
showsUp: Specificity fights that end in !important.
Cascade layers, which let you order whole stylesheets explicitly.
tradeoffs: Source order matters, so bundling changes can change the result.
Raising specificity to win once makes the next override harder.

terms.name: Design tokens
terms.definition: Named values for colour, spacing, type and motion that act as the single source for a visual system.
showsUp: CSS custom properties and theme files.
Hand-off between design tools and code.
tradeoffs: Tokens named after appearance (blue-500) resist theming; names by role (surface, accent) survive it.
Too many tokens recreate the inconsistency they were meant to remove.

areas.name: Performance
areas.definition: How quickly an interface loads, responds to input and stays visually stable on real devices.
showsUp: Bundle budgets and lab or field measurements.
Conversion and retention numbers.
tradeoffs: A fast developer laptop hides problems a mid-range phone will show.
Optimising a metric is not the same as improving the experience.

terms.name: Code splitting
terms.definition: Breaking a JavaScript bundle into chunks that load only when the route or feature that needs them is used.
showsUp: Dynamic import() and route-level lazy loading.
Heavy editors, charts or maps loaded on demand.
tradeoffs: Each split adds a network round trip at the moment of use.
Too many small chunks can be slower than one medium one.

terms.name: Core Web Vitals
terms.definition: Google's field metrics for loading (LCP), responsiveness (INP) and visual stability (CLS).
showsUp: Search ranking signals and performance dashboards.
Real-user monitoring, split by device and connection.
tradeoffs: Lab scores and field data often disagree; field data is what counts.
The 75th percentile hides your slowest users.

fields.name: Backend
fields.definition: The code that runs on machines you control, owning business rules, data access and communication with other systems.
showsUp: Request handlers, background workers and scheduled jobs.
Any rule that must hold no matter which client calls it.
tradeoffs: It is the last line of defence, so it cannot trust any client.
Its failures are shared by every user at once.

areas.name: APIs
areas.definition: The contract a service exposes so other programs can call it without knowing how it works inside.
showsUp: Between frontend and backend, and between services.
Public integrations for partners and customers.
tradeoffs: Once published, a contract is expensive to change.
An API shaped around your database leaks your internals.

terms.name: REST
terms.definition: An API style that models a system as resources addressed by URLs and manipulated with standard HTTP methods.
showsUp: Most public web APIs.
Anywhere HTTP caching and status codes carry meaning.
tradeoffs: Clients often over-fetch, or need several round trips for one screen.
Operations that are not create, read, update or delete fit awkwardly.

terms.name: GraphQL
terms.definition: A query language where the client specifies exactly which fields it wants from a typed schema, in one request.
showsUp: Apps with many screens reading overlapping data.
A gateway in front of several backend services.
tradeoffs: Naive resolvers produce N+1 queries; batching is required.
HTTP caching and rate limiting need extra design.

areas.name: Auth
areas.definition: Establishing who a caller is (authentication) and what they are allowed to do (authorisation).
showsUp: Login flows, API keys and service-to-service calls.
Every endpoint that returns someone's data.
tradeoffs: Authentication without per-resource authorisation is the commonest serious bug.
Building your own is rarely worth the risk.

terms.name: OAuth
terms.definition: A protocol that lets a user grant an application limited access to their account without sharing a password.
showsUp: Sign in with Google or GitHub buttons.
Third-party apps acting on a user's behalf.
tradeoffs: It is delegation, not identity; OpenID Connect adds the identity layer.
Flow choice matters: the wrong one for a public client leaks tokens.

terms.name: Sessions
terms.definition: Server-held state tied to an opaque identifier, usually in a cookie, that remembers a logged-in user between requests.
showsUp: Traditional web apps and many modern ones.
The alternative people weigh against stateless tokens.
tradeoffs: Needs a shared store once you run more than one server.
Easy to revoke, which self-contained tokens are not.

areas.name: Concurrency
areas.definition: Making progress on several tasks in overlapping time, whether or not they run at the same instant.
showsUp: Servers handling many requests at once.
Any code path that waits on a network or disk.
tradeoffs: Shared mutable state is where the bugs live.
Failures are timing-dependent and hard to reproduce.

terms.name: Event loop
terms.definition: A single thread that repeatedly takes ready tasks from a queue and runs each to completion, never blocking on I/O.
showsUp: Node.js, browsers and Python's asyncio.
Services that are mostly waiting on other services.
tradeoffs: One CPU-heavy task stalls every other request.
Forgotten awaits fail silently or out of order.

terms.name: Threads
terms.definition: Independent paths of execution within one process that share memory and can run in parallel on multiple cores.
showsUp: Java, Go and Rust servers; worker pools.
CPU-bound work such as image processing.
tradeoffs: Shared memory needs locks, which bring deadlocks and contention.
Each thread has a memory cost, so thousands of idle ones add up.

areas.name: Messaging
areas.definition: Passing work or notifications between systems without the sender waiting for the receiver to finish.
showsUp: Background jobs, emails and integrations.
Decoupling services that scale at different rates.
tradeoffs: You trade immediate errors for delayed, harder-to-see ones.
Delivery is usually at-least-once, so duplicates are normal.

terms.name: Queues
terms.definition: A buffer that holds messages until a consumer is ready, smoothing bursts and letting work survive restarts.
showsUp: SQS, RabbitMQ and Redis-backed job runners.
Anything slow moved out of the request path.
tradeoffs: Ordering is often not guaranteed unless you pay for it.
A poison message can block or loop without a dead-letter queue.

terms.name: Webhooks
terms.definition: An HTTP request a service sends to your URL when something happens, so you do not have to poll for changes.
showsUp: Payment, source control and messaging platforms.
Triggering pipelines from external events.
tradeoffs: They arrive late, twice or out of order; handlers must cope.
You must verify the signature, or anyone can post fake events.

fields.name: Data
fields.definition: How information is stored, shaped, moved and kept correct over the life of a system.
showsUp: Databases, warehouses, caches and files.
Most outages and most migrations.
tradeoffs: Data outlives the code that wrote it.
Mistakes here are the hardest to undo.

areas.name: Storage
areas.definition: The engines that persist data and the guarantees they make about reading it back.
showsUp: Choosing a database and tuning queries.
Backups, replication and recovery.
tradeoffs: Stronger guarantees usually cost throughput or availability.
The access pattern, not the data size, should drive the choice.

terms.name: Indexes
terms.definition: An auxiliary structure, usually a B-tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.
showsUp: WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY on large tables.
Query plans that switch from scan to seek.
tradeoffs: Every index slows writes and takes space.
Column order in a composite index decides which queries can use it.

terms.name: Transactions
terms.definition: A group of operations the database treats as one unit: all take effect or none do.
showsUp: Moving money, placing orders, anything multi-step.
Isolation levels that decide what concurrent readers see.
tradeoffs: Long transactions hold locks and block others.
The default isolation level permits anomalies many developers assume are impossible.

areas.name: Modelling
areas.definition: Deciding what entities exist, how they relate and what shape their records take.
showsUp: The first schema and every migration after it.
API shapes, which tend to mirror the model.
tradeoffs: A model tuned for writing is rarely ideal for reading.
Early modelling mistakes compound with every feature.

terms.name: Normalisation
terms.definition: Organising tables so each fact is stored once, removing redundancy and the update anomalies it causes.
showsUp: Relational schema design.
Deciding whether to copy a customer name onto each order.
tradeoffs: More joins at read time.
Deliberate denormalisation is fine; accidental duplication is not.

terms.name: Schemas
terms.definition: A formal description of the structure and types data must follow, enforced by a database or a validator.
showsUp: Table definitions, JSON Schema, Protobuf and Avro.
Contracts between producers and consumers of events.
tradeoffs: Schemaless stores still have a schema; it just lives in application code.
Changes must stay compatible while old and new code run together.

areas.name: Pipelines
areas.definition: Automated flows that move data from where it is produced to where it is analysed or served.
showsUp: Analytics, reporting and machine-learning features.
Syncing operational data into search or a warehouse.
tradeoffs: Silent data errors are worse than crashes.
Reprocessing history must be possible, so steps should be repeatable.

terms.name: ETL
terms.definition: Extract, transform, load: pulling data from sources, reshaping it and writing it to a destination, typically in batches.
showsUp: Nightly warehouse loads.
Its variant ELT, which loads raw data first and transforms in the warehouse.
tradeoffs: Results are only as fresh as the last run.
Upstream schema changes break jobs without warning.

terms.name: Streaming
terms.definition: Processing records continuously as they arrive, instead of waiting to collect them into batches.
showsUp: Kafka, Kinesis and Flink.
Fraud checks, live dashboards and change data capture.
tradeoffs: Late and out-of-order events force you to reason about time explicitly.
Operationally heavier than batch; use it when freshness pays for it.

areas.name: Caching
areas.definition: Keeping a copy of an expensive result closer to where it is needed, so repeat requests are cheaper.
showsUp: CDNs, Redis, in-process memoisation and HTTP headers.
In front of slow queries and rate-limited APIs.
tradeoffs: You accept some staleness in exchange for speed.
A cache that hides a slow system makes its outage worse.

terms.name: Invalidation
terms.definition: Removing or updating cached entries when the underlying data changes, so readers stop seeing stale values.
showsUp: Purging a CDN after a deploy.
Deleting a cache key after a write.
tradeoffs: Knowing every key affected by a change is the hard part.
Races between a write and a concurrent refill can re-cache old data.

terms.name: TTL
terms.definition: Time to live: how long a cached entry is considered fresh before it expires and must be fetched again.
showsUp: DNS records, Cache-Control max-age and Redis EXPIRE.
The simplest invalidation strategy available.
tradeoffs: Too short wastes the cache; too long serves stale data.
Many keys expiring together cause a stampede on the origin.

fields.name: AI
fields.definition: Systems whose behaviour is learned from data instead of written as explicit rules.
showsUp: Search, recommendations, assistants and code tools.
Features where exact rules are impractical to write.
tradeoffs: Outputs are probabilistic, so testing means measuring, not asserting.
Cost and latency scale with usage in ways ordinary code does not.

areas.name: Models
areas.definition: The learned functions themselves: their architecture, what they take in and what they produce.
showsUp: Choosing between hosted and self-run models.
Matching model size to task difficulty.
tradeoffs: Larger models are more capable, slower and costlier.
A model's knowledge stops at its training cutoff.

terms.name: Transformers
terms.definition: A neural network architecture that uses attention to relate every token in a sequence to every other token.
showsUp: Nearly all current language models.
Vision, audio and protein models built on the same design.
tradeoffs: Attention cost grows quickly with sequence length.
No built-in memory beyond what fits in the input.

terms.name: Embeddings
terms.definition: Vectors that place text, images or other items in a space where similar meanings sit close together.
showsUp: Semantic search, clustering and recommendations.
The retrieval step of RAG.
tradeoffs: Vectors from different models are not comparable; changing model means re-embedding.
Similar is not the same as relevant or correct.

areas.name: Training
areas.definition: Adjusting a model's weights on data so its outputs improve on a chosen objective.
showsUp: Building a model, or adapting an existing one.
Deciding whether prompting alone is enough.
tradeoffs: Data quality limits the result more than technique does.
It is slow and costly to iterate compared with changing a prompt.

terms.name: Fine-tuning
terms.definition: Continuing to train a pre-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset to change its behaviour.
showsUp: Enforcing a consistent format, tone or narrow skill.
Making a small model match a large one on one task.
tradeoffs: It teaches behaviour better than facts; use retrieval for knowledge.
You own a model version that must be re-tuned when the base changes.

terms.name: Evaluation
terms.definition: Measuring model quality on a fixed set of cases, so changes can be compared instead of judged by feel.
showsUp: Before shipping a prompt or model change.
Regression suites built from real failures.
tradeoffs: Automatic graders, including model graders, need checking against human judgement.
A test set you tune against stops telling you the truth.

areas.name: Inference
areas.definition: Running a trained model to produce an output for a given input.
showsUp: Every API call to a model.
Latency, throughput and cost planning.
tradeoffs: Output is generated token by token, so long answers are slow answers.
Sampling settings trade consistency for variety.

terms.name: Tokens
terms.definition: The sub-word units a language model reads and writes; text is split into them before processing.
showsUp: Pricing, rate limits and length limits.
Odd behaviour with rare words, numbers or non-English text.
tradeoffs: Token count is not word count and differs between models.
Output tokens usually cost more than input tokens.

terms.name: Context window
terms.definition: The maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once, covering instructions, history, documents and its reply.
showsUp: Long conversations and large documents.
Deciding what to include, summarise or retrieve.
tradeoffs: Filling it raises cost and latency on every call.
Models attend less reliably to material buried in very long inputs.

areas.name: Agents
areas.definition: Systems where a model decides which actions to take in a loop, using the results to choose its next step.
showsUp: Coding assistants, research tools and workflow automation.
Tasks whose steps cannot be fixed in advance.
tradeoffs: Errors compound across steps.
More autonomy needs tighter permissions and better logging.

terms.name: Tool use
terms.definition: Letting a model request calls to functions you define, with your code executing them and returning the results.
showsUp: Looking up live data, running code, calling internal APIs.
Structured output via a schema.
tradeoffs: Tool descriptions are prompts; vague ones cause wrong calls.
Tool results are untrusted input and can carry injected instructions.

terms.name: RAG
terms.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation: fetching relevant documents at request time and giving them to the model as context.
showsUp: Question answering over private or recent documents.
Answers that need citations.
tradeoffs: Answer quality is capped by retrieval quality.
Chunking and ranking choices matter more than the vector database.

fields.name: Infrastructure
fields.definition: The machines, networks and automation that run software and get changes to it safely.
showsUp: Cloud accounts, clusters and deployment pipelines.
The on-call rota.
tradeoffs: Flexibility and operational burden rise together.
The bill is a design output, not an afterthought.

areas.name: Compute
areas.definition: Where and how code actually executes, and who manages the layers beneath it.
showsUp: Choosing between virtual machines, containers and functions.
Capacity and scaling decisions.
tradeoffs: More managed means less control and less to maintain.
Scaling to zero saves money and adds start-up delay.

terms.name: Containers
terms.definition: A packaged process with its dependencies, isolated by the kernel but sharing the host operating system.
showsUp: Docker images and Kubernetes pods.
Making development, CI and production run the same thing.
tradeoffs: Isolation is weaker than a virtual machine's.
Large images slow builds, pulls and cold starts.

terms.name: Serverless
terms.definition: Running code on demand without managing servers, billed per invocation and scaled automatically by the provider.
showsUp: Functions behind HTTP endpoints, queues and schedules.
Spiky or low-volume workloads.
tradeoffs: Cold starts add latency to the first request.
Time limits and no local state rule out long-running or connection-heavy work.

areas.name: Networking
areas.definition: How requests find the right machine and travel there reliably and securely.
showsUp: Domains, certificates, firewalls and private networks.
Problems that look like application bugs but are not.
tradeoffs: Every hop adds latency and a failure point.
Misconfiguration tends to fail closed or wide open.

terms.name: DNS
terms.definition: The system that translates domain names into the IP addresses machines use to reach each other.
showsUp: Pointing a domain at a host; mail and verification records.
Failover and geographic routing.
tradeoffs: Changes spread only as fast as cached records expire.
It is a common single point of failure in large outages.

terms.name: Load balancing
terms.definition: Distributing incoming requests across several servers so no one of them is overwhelmed and failures are routed around.
showsUp: In front of any service with more than one instance.
Zero-downtime deploys and health checks.
tradeoffs: Sticky sessions simplify state and undermine even distribution.
A health check that is too shallow keeps sending traffic to a broken instance.

areas.name: Delivery
areas.definition: The path a change takes from a commit to running in production, and how risk is controlled along it.
showsUp: Build pipelines and release processes.
How quickly a fix can reach users.
tradeoffs: Speed and safety are both products of automation, not opposites.
A slow pipeline encourages large, risky batches.

terms.name: CI/CD
terms.definition: Continuous integration and delivery: automatically building, testing and releasing every change through a repeatable pipeline.
showsUp: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and similar.
Merge checks and automated deploys.
tradeoffs: Flaky tests teach people to ignore red builds.
Pipelines hold powerful credentials and need securing like production.

terms.name: Blue-green deploys
terms.definition: Running the new version beside the old one, then switching all traffic at once, with the old kept ready for rollback.
showsUp: Releases that need instant rollback.
Its gradual cousin, the canary release.
tradeoffs: You pay for two environments during the switch.
Database changes must work with both versions at once.

areas.name: Observability
areas.definition: Being able to work out what a system is doing inside from the signals it emits.
showsUp: Dashboards, alerts and incident investigation.
Answering questions you did not anticipate.
tradeoffs: Telemetry volume becomes a significant cost.
Alerts nobody acts on train people to ignore alerts.

terms.name: Tracing
terms.definition: Following one request across every service it touches, recording the timing of each step as linked spans.
showsUp: Finding which hop made a request slow.
OpenTelemetry instrumentation.
tradeoffs: Context must be passed through every call, including queues.
Sampling keeps cost down and can drop the trace you needed.

terms.name: Metrics
terms.definition: Numeric measurements aggregated over time, such as request rate, error rate and latency percentiles.
showsUp: Dashboards, alerts and service level objectives.
Capacity planning.
tradeoffs: Averages hide the slow tail; use percentiles.
High-cardinality labels, like user IDs, blow up storage.

fields.name: Security
fields.definition: Keeping systems and data confidential, intact and available in the presence of people trying to misuse them.
showsUp: Design reviews, dependency updates and incident response.
Every boundary where untrusted input enters.
tradeoffs: Controls that add too much friction get bypassed.
Attackers need one gap; defenders need to cover all of them.

areas.name: Identity
areas.definition: Knowing which person or service is acting, and limiting what that identity can reach.
showsUp: Single sign-on, service accounts and cloud roles.
Access reviews and offboarding.
tradeoffs: Shared accounts destroy accountability.
Permissions accumulate unless someone removes them.

terms.name: MFA
terms.definition: Multi-factor authentication: requiring a second proof, such as a device or key, in addition to a password.
showsUp: Login for admin consoles, email and source control.
Passkeys and hardware security keys.
tradeoffs: SMS and push prompts can be phished or approved by a tired user.
Account recovery is often the weakest path around it.

terms.name: Least privilege
terms.definition: Granting each identity only the permissions it needs for its task, and nothing more.
showsUp: Cloud access policies and database roles.
Scoped API tokens.
tradeoffs: Tight policies take effort to write and maintain.
Wildcard grants added to unblock someone tend to stay.

areas.name: Cryptography
areas.definition: Mathematical techniques for keeping data secret, detecting tampering and proving who sent it.
showsUp: HTTPS, password storage, signed tokens and disk encryption.
Anywhere data crosses a network you do not control.
tradeoffs: Use vetted libraries; hand-rolled schemes fail in subtle ways.
Key management is harder than the algorithms.

terms.name: Hashing
terms.definition: A one-way function that maps any input to a fixed-size value, so the input cannot practically be recovered.
showsUp: Password storage, file integrity checks and content addressing.
Git commit identifiers.
tradeoffs: Passwords need a deliberately slow, salted hash such as Argon2 or bcrypt.
Fast general-purpose hashes are easy to brute-force.

terms.name: TLS
terms.definition: The protocol that encrypts traffic between two parties and verifies the server's identity with a certificate.
showsUp: Every HTTPS connection.
Service-to-service calls, sometimes with certificates on both sides.
tradeoffs: Expired certificates are a classic self-inflicted outage.
Encryption ends at the load balancer unless you extend it.

areas.name: Threats
areas.definition: The recurring ways software is attacked, most of which abuse trust in input.
showsUp: Vulnerability reports and penetration tests.
The OWASP Top Ten.
tradeoffs: The same few classes account for most real incidents.
Frameworks prevent many by default until you opt out.

terms.name: Injection
terms.definition: Untrusted input being interpreted as code or commands because it was mixed into a query or instruction.
showsUp: SQL built by string concatenation; shell commands with user input.
Prompt injection against language models.
tradeoffs: Parameterised queries remove the SQL form entirely.
Filtering bad input is weaker than separating data from code.

terms.name: XSS
terms.definition: Cross-site scripting: an attacker's script running in another user's browser under your site's origin.
showsUp: User content rendered as HTML without escaping.
Stolen sessions and actions taken as the victim.
tradeoffs: Escaping must match the context: HTML, attribute, URL or script.
A content security policy limits damage; it does not replace escaping.

areas.name: Defence
areas.definition: The practices that reduce the chance of a breach and limit the damage when one happens.
showsUp: Design reviews, patching and incident drills.
Compliance audits.
tradeoffs: Layered controls cost more and fail less.
Detection you never test may not work when needed.

terms.name: Threat modelling
terms.definition: Systematically asking what could go wrong in a design, who would do it and what would stop them.
showsUp: Design reviews for new features.
Data flow diagrams with trust boundaries marked.
tradeoffs: Done once and filed away, it goes stale with the first redesign.
A short session beats a perfect document nobody writes.

terms.name: Secrets management
terms.definition: Storing, distributing and rotating credentials so they never sit in code, images or logs.
showsUp: Vault services and environment injection at deploy time.
Scanners that block commits containing keys.
tradeoffs: A secret committed once is in history; rotate it, do not just delete it.
Rotation that has never been practised will break something.

fields.name: Architecture
fields.definition: The large-scale decisions about how a system is divided and how its parts communicate.
showsUp: Design documents and whiteboard sessions.
The things that are expensive to change later.
tradeoffs: Every choice optimises for some qualities at the cost of others.
Team structure shapes it as much as technology does.

areas.name: Structure
areas.definition: Where the boundaries between parts of a system are drawn, and what is deployed together.
showsUp: Repository layout and service ownership.
Deciding when to split or merge components.
tradeoffs: Boundaries in the wrong place cost more than no boundaries.
Splitting moves complexity from code into the network.

terms.name: Monolith
terms.definition: An application built and deployed as a single unit, with modules calling each other in-process.
showsUp: Most products at the start, and many at scale.
The modular monolith, with enforced internal boundaries.
tradeoffs: Simple to run and refactor; one bad deploy affects everything.
Without discipline, modules become tangled.

terms.name: Microservices
terms.definition: A system split into small services that are deployed independently and communicate over the network.
showsUp: Organisations with many teams shipping separately.
Parts with very different scaling or reliability needs.
tradeoffs: You take on distributed-systems problems: partial failure, versioning, tracing.
Services that must deploy together are a monolith with extra latency.

areas.name: Distribution
areas.definition: What changes when a system runs on several machines that can fail or lose contact independently.
showsUp: Replicated databases and multi-region deployments.
Any call that crosses a network.
tradeoffs: A timeout cannot tell you whether the other side did the work.
Clocks on different machines disagree.

terms.name: Consensus
terms.definition: Getting a group of machines to agree on a single value or ordering even when some of them fail.
showsUp: Raft and Paxos inside etcd, ZooKeeper and many databases.
Leader election and distributed locks.
tradeoffs: Needs a majority to be reachable, so it stops during some partitions.
Every agreed write costs network round trips.

terms.name: CAP theorem
terms.definition: During a network partition, a distributed store must give up either consistency or availability; it cannot keep both.
showsUp: Choosing and configuring replicated databases.
Deciding what a user sees when a region is cut off.
tradeoffs: It says nothing about normal operation, where latency is the real trade.
Real systems choose per operation, not once for the whole system.

areas.name: Resilience
areas.definition: Designing so that the failure of one part degrades the system instead of taking it down.
showsUp: Timeouts, retries and fallbacks.
Post-incident reviews.
tradeoffs: Retries without limits turn a blip into an outage.
Fallback paths that are never exercised usually do not work.

terms.name: Idempotency
terms.definition: An operation that produces the same result whether it runs once or many times.
showsUp: Payment APIs that accept an idempotency key.
Queue consumers that may receive a message twice.
tradeoffs: You need somewhere to store the keys, and a rule for expiring them.
Retries are only safe if every step downstream is idempotent too.

terms.name: Circuit breaker
terms.definition: A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency for a while, failing fast instead of piling up waiting requests.
showsUp: Service clients and API gateways.
Protecting thread pools and connection limits.
tradeoffs: Thresholds need tuning; too sensitive and it trips on noise.
You still have to decide what to return while it is open.

areas.name: Patterns
areas.definition: Named, reusable solutions to recurring design problems, each with known costs.
showsUp: Design discussions, as shared vocabulary.
Framework and library documentation.
tradeoffs: A pattern applied without its problem is just complexity.
Names help communication and can hide disagreement about details.

terms.name: Event sourcing
terms.definition: Storing every change as an immutable event and deriving current state by replaying them.
showsUp: Ledgers, audit-heavy domains and collaborative editing.
Systems that need to answer what the state was at a past time.
tradeoffs: Event shapes are permanent, so evolving them takes care.
Reads need separately built projections, which lag behind writes.

terms.name: CQRS
terms.definition: Command query responsibility segregation: using separate models, and often separate stores, for writes and reads.
showsUp: Read-heavy systems with complex write rules.
Alongside event sourcing, though neither requires the other.
tradeoffs: The read side is eventually consistent with the write side.
Two models to maintain; overkill for simple record-keeping.

fields.name: Craft
fields.definition: The everyday practices that keep code correct, understandable and safe to change.
showsUp: Pull requests, test suites and team conventions.
How long a new joiner takes to ship.
tradeoffs: The pay-off is long-term and easy to defer.
Practice followed as ritual loses its purpose.

areas.name: Testing
areas.definition: Running code against known expectations to catch mistakes before users do.
showsUp: Local development and CI pipelines.
Refactoring with confidence.
tradeoffs: Tests are code and carry maintenance cost.
Coverage measures what ran, not what was checked.

terms.name: Unit tests
terms.definition: Tests that check one small piece of logic in isolation, quickly and without external systems.
showsUp: Pure functions, parsers and business rules.
The fast feedback loop while writing code.
tradeoffs: Heavy mocking tests the mocks, not the behaviour.
Tests tied to implementation details break on every refactor.

terms.name: Integration tests
terms.definition: Tests that exercise several components together, including real databases, queues or HTTP boundaries.
showsUp: API endpoints tested against a real database.
Contract checks between services.
tradeoffs: Slower and harder to keep deterministic.
They find the bugs unit tests cannot: wiring, configuration and queries.

areas.name: Version control
areas.definition: Recording every change to a codebase so work can be reviewed, combined and undone.
showsUp: Git, in almost every project.
Release tagging and incident archaeology.
tradeoffs: History is only useful if commits are coherent.
Large binary files and generated code fit poorly.

terms.name: Branching
terms.definition: Creating an independent line of commits so work can proceed without affecting the main line until merged.
showsUp: Feature branches and pull requests.
Trunk-based development, which keeps branches very short.
tradeoffs: Long-lived branches drift and produce painful merges.
Many release branches multiply the places a fix must land.

terms.name: Rebase
terms.definition: Replaying your commits on top of another branch's tip, producing a linear history with new commit identifiers.
showsUp: Updating a feature branch before merging.
Interactive rebase to tidy commits before review.
tradeoffs: Rewriting commits others have pulled causes confusion and lost work.
Conflicts are resolved commit by commit, which can repeat effort.

areas.name: Quality
areas.definition: Keeping code readable and well-structured so the next change is as cheap as the last.
showsUp: Code review, linting and style guides.
The speed at which a team can still move in year three.
tradeoffs: Polish beyond what the code's lifetime justifies is waste.
Standards work only if tooling enforces them.

terms.name: Refactoring
terms.definition: Changing the internal structure of code without changing its observable behaviour.
showsUp: Before adding a feature, to make room for it.
Extracting, renaming and removing duplication.
tradeoffs: Without tests you cannot tell whether behaviour was preserved.
Mixing it with feature changes makes both hard to review.

terms.name: Code review
terms.definition: Having another person read a change before it merges, to catch defects and spread knowledge.
showsUp: Pull requests and merge requests.
Onboarding, as a way to learn a codebase.
tradeoffs: Large changes get shallow reviews; keep them small.
Slow reviews push people toward bigger batches.

areas.name: Planning
areas.definition: Deciding what to build, in what order, and how to release it with controlled risk.
showsUp: Roadmaps, estimates and release plans.
Negotiation between speed now and speed later.
tradeoffs: Estimates are forecasts and get treated as promises.
Shortcuts are loans; someone pays the interest.

terms.name: Tech debt
terms.definition: The future cost created by choosing a quicker solution now over a better one that would take longer.
showsUp: Areas of the code everyone avoids touching.
Features that take longer each quarter.
tradeoffs: Taken deliberately and repaid, it is a useful tool.
Untracked, it compounds until a rewrite looks tempting.

terms.name: Feature flags
terms.definition: Runtime switches that turn code paths on or off without a deploy, often per user or percentage.
showsUp: Gradual rollouts, experiments and kill switches.
Merging unfinished work safely to the main branch.
tradeoffs: Every flag doubles the states to test.
Flags left in after launch become dead code with live risk.
